chapter.title: Buying the whole bazaar at once

cards.body:
Walking the bazaar, you could pick one shop and bet on it. Or you could buy a **basket with a slice of all 50 big shops** inside, in one trip.

That basket is an *index fund*: a fund that copies the Nifty 50 list exactly, with no picking and no opinions. Picture a steel tiffin carrier with 50 small compartments. You own one carrier.
cards.simpler:
Imagine a bazaar with 50 big shops. You could pick one shop and hope it does well. Or you could buy a **basket holding a small slice of all 50 shops** in one trip.

That basket is called an index fund. It copies the Nifty 50 list exactly, so nobody has to choose. Think of a steel tiffin carrier with 50 small boxes inside. You own the whole carrier.

cards.prompt: Priya has ₹500 and 10 minutes before dinner. She wants to own a tiny bit of all 50 Nifty companies tonight. What gets her there?

options.text: Buy 1 share each of all 50 companies
Put ₹500 into a Nifty 50 index fund
Buy 1 share of the biggest Nifty company

whyNot.a: That's 50 separate trades, not one basket: a single share of some Nifty companies costs more than ₹500 on its own.
whyNot.c: That's one shop, not the whole bazaar: the index fund is the thing that holds all 50.

cards.reteach: An index fund is one purchase that holds all 50 Nifty shops in the same proportions as the index. You don't pick, and you don't need enough money for 50 separate shares. ₹500 buys a tiny slice of the whole basket.

cards.title: Two kinds of basket
cards.body:
A *mutual fund* is a basket of shares that many people pay into together, run by a fund company. There are two main kinds.

An *index fund* just copies a list. A Nifty 50 index fund holds the same 50 shops, in the same proportions, as the Nifty 50 board. Nobody decides anything. If the index rises 1%, your basket rises about 1%.

An *active fund* hires a shopper, called a *fund manager*, to pick which shops to buy and when, hoping to beat the index. **Copying is cheap, hiring a shopper costs more**, and you pay that cost whether or not they beat it.
cards.simpler:
A mutual fund is a basket of shares many people pay into together. An index fund copies a list. A Nifty 50 index fund holds the same 50 shops, in the same amounts, as the Nifty 50 board. Nobody picks anything.

An active fund hires someone, called a fund manager, to choose shops and try to beat the index. **Copying is cheap, hiring a shopper costs more**, and you pay that cost even if they fail.

cards.title: Ravi's two baskets
cards.body:
Ravi puts ₹10,000 into two funds in January. Fund A is a Nifty 50 index fund charging 0.2% a year. Fund B has a well-known manager and charges 1.5% a year.

By December both baskets have grown 12% before fees. Fund A leaves Ravi with about ₹11,180. Fund B leaves him about ₹11,030. The **manager did exactly as well as the index**, and Ravi paid ₹150 for the company.
cards.simpler:
Ravi puts ₹10,000 into two funds in January. Fund A copies the Nifty 50 and charges 0.2% a year. Fund B has a famous manager and charges 1.5% a year.

By December both have grown 12% before fees. Fund A leaves Ravi with about ₹11,180. Fund B leaves him with about ₹11,030. The **manager did exactly as well as the index**, and Ravi paid ₹150 extra for the company.

cards.prompt: Meena's broker app shows two Nifty 50 index funds. Both track the same 50 companies. One shows an expense ratio of 0.1%, the other 0.6%. Which should she pick?

options.text: The 0.6% one, because a higher fee means a better manager
The 0.1% one, because they hold the same shops and the fee is the only difference
Either, since the fee is paid by the fund company, not by her

whyNot.a: That's active-fund thinking applied to an index fund: both copy the same list, so nobody is picking anything to pay extra for.
whyNot.c: That's mixing up who the fee is paid to with where it comes from: the expense ratio is shaved off your money, every year.

cards.reteach: The expense ratio is the yearly slice taken from your money to run the fund. Two index funds copying the same 50 shops will grow the same before fees. So the one with the lower fee leaves you more.

cards.title: SIP, and the fee you never see
cards.body:
A *SIP*, short for systematic investment plan, is a standing instruction: a fixed amount, say ₹1,000, leaves your bank on a fixed date each month and buys fund units. When prices are high, ₹1,000 buys fewer units. When prices dip, it buys more. You stop guessing the right day.

The *expense ratio* is the yearly fee, shown as a percentage of your money. You never get a bill. It's quietly shaved off the fund's value a little every day. **A 1% fee on ₹1 lakh is ₹1,000 gone every year**, and it grows as your money grows.
cards.simpler:
A SIP, or systematic investment plan, is a standing order. A fixed amount, say ₹1,000, leaves your bank each month and buys fund units. High prices mean fewer units, low prices mean more. You stop guessing the right day.

The expense ratio is the yearly fee, shown as a percentage. It is quietly shaved off the fund a little each day. **A 1% fee on ₹1 lakh is ₹1,000 gone every year**, and it grows with your money.

cards.body:
Arjun sets up a ₹2,000 SIP, watches the Nifty fall 4% in a week, and pauses it "until things calm down". That month's ₹2,000 would have bought more units than any month before.

Spot it in yourself: if you're stopping a SIP because prices fell, you're doing **the one thing a SIP exists to stop you doing**.
cards.simpler:
Arjun sets up a ₹2,000 SIP. Then the Nifty falls 4% in one week. Arjun pauses it until things calm down. But that month's ₹2,000 would have bought more units than any month before, because prices were lower.

Check yourself for this. If you are stopping a SIP because prices fell, you are doing **the one thing a SIP exists to stop you doing**.

cards.prompt: Your cousin says: "Index funds are for lazy people. A fund manager works for you all day, so of course that fund does better." What's the catch?

options.text: Index funds also have a manager, so they cost the same anyway
The manager's fee comes out of your money every year, whether or not they beat the index
SIPs don't work with active funds, so you'd have to invest a lump sum

whyNot.a: That's the opposite of how an index fund works: it copies a list, needs no picker, and usually charges far less.
whyNot.c: That's mixing up SIP with fund type: a SIP is just a monthly auto-payment and works with either kind of fund.

cards.reteach: Hiring a shopper is not free. An active fund charges a higher expense ratio every year, taken from your money, so the manager has to beat the index by more than that fee just for you to break even. You can't know in advance which managers will.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
An index fund buys you a slice of all 50 Nifty shops in one go, and a SIP buys a fixed amount of it every month so you never have to pick the day.

The one number to check before you start is **the expense ratio**, the yearly fee shaved off your money, and lower is better.
cards.simpler:
An index fund buys you a small slice of all 50 Nifty shops in one go. A SIP buys a fixed amount of it every month, so you never have to pick the day.

Before you start, check one number: **the expense ratio**. That is the yearly fee quietly taken off your money. Lower is better.

cards.body: Open your broker app, search "Nifty 50 index fund", and open any two. Find the expense ratio on each page and write both numbers down. **Don't buy anything yet.**
cards.simpler: Open your broker app and search for "Nifty 50 index fund". Open any two of the results. On each page, find the expense ratio, the yearly fee shown as a percentage. Write both numbers down side by side. That is the whole task for now. **Don't buy anything yet.**

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now set up a monthly SIP in a Nifty 50 index fund and say what expense ratio you are paying.
